clue.text: Writer filling dictionary made a start

indicators.note: the writer sits inside the dictionary, filling it up

parts.note: the OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
a pen is the thing you write with

explanation.surface: An author starts work on a dictionary, getting things under way.
explanation.definitionFit: To open is to begin, so 'opened' is a past-tense synonym for began or made a start.

clue.text: Don briefly embraces Latin underworld boss

indicators.note: the shortened word holds the Latin abbreviation inside its arms
cut short, so the last letter of the phrase for 'don' is dropped

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on

explanation.surface: A Mafia don hugging a Latin-speaking crime boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a Mafia boss, steering towards the definition, but it is the verb meaning to wear.
explanation.definitionFit: Pluto is the Roman god who rules the realm of the dead, the lord of the underworld.

clue.text: Type of crocus which lord first saw on honeymoon?

definitions.meaning: the plain sense: the autumn crocus, Colchicum, is popularly called this because its flowers appear without leaves

definitions.text: which lord first saw on honeymoon
definitions.meaning: the cheeky sense: what a new husband of rank first sees on the wedding night is his undressed bride

explanation.surface: A botanical quiz about a flower that a nobleman spotted on his wedding trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant name read literally describes a wife without clothes, which is what the bridegroom lord sees on honeymoon.
explanation.definitionFit: Colchicum autumnale, the meadow saffron, bears bare flowers without leaves and so is commonly nicknamed after an unclothed woman.

clue.text: Flipping dog one had to extract from a hole

indicators.note: flipped over, so the whole string of letters is read backwards, upwards in this down light

parts.note: a pug is a small breed of dog
the contraction 'd stands for had

explanation.surface: A dog that had to be pulled out of a burrow, with a mild oath thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, but it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig something up is to unearth it, bringing it out of the ground or a hole.

clue.text: Part of Manchester that sounds suitable for Cockney's poker game?

indicators.note: the answer is said to sound like the poker game as spoken

parts.note: Texas hold 'em is a popular poker game, and a Cockney Londoner drops the aitch to say 'old 'em

explanation.surface: A district near Manchester that a Londoner would say like the name of a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys drop initial H, so hold 'em becomes 'old 'em, which is how the town's name is said.
explanation.definitionFit: Oldham is a town and borough within Greater Manchester, the metropolitan county in north-west England.

clue.text: Priest's assistant remained behind collecting dues regularly

parts.note: lay is the past tense of lie, which can mean to stay or remain

indicators.note: the word for behind gathers the other letters inside it

parts.note: the rear is what is behind

indicators.note: every other letter of the word taken, starting from the first

parts.note: taken as written for the letter selection

explanation.surface: A cleric's helper stayed late to gather the subscriptions.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay reader is a church member, not ordained, licensed to lead services and assist the clergy.

clue.text: Hot dog with no pee forbidden drink

indicators.note: the dog is left without one letter

parts.note: a pooch is an informal word for a dog
pee spells out the sound of the letter P

explanation.surface: A hot dog that isn't allowed to relieve itself, oddly paired with banned liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot dog' looks like a sausage in a bun, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooch is slang for illicit or bootleg liquor, the kind sold during Prohibition when alcohol was banned.

clue.text: Beggar's admission of failure as a tinker?

parts.note: a tinker mends pots and pans, so his trade is to repair
saying 'I can't' admits you are unable to do something

explanation.surface: A beggar confessing he has failed as a tinker, the travelling repairman.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as a tinker's confession: 'mend? I can't'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant is someone who lives by begging, especially a friar of a begging order.

clue.text: Propose new brewery worker makes waste disposal unit

indicators.note: the letters are made into something new, a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
a cooper makes the wooden barrels a brewery uses

explanation.surface: Someone suggests that a new man at the brewery builds a rubbish bin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste disposal unit' suggests a kitchen sink grinder; here it is the scoop for dog mess.
explanation.definitionFit: A pooper-scooper is a small implement for picking up and disposing of dog droppings, humorously called a unit for waste.

clue.text: Dollar one lost in American's car

indicators.note: the letter for one goes missing from the car's name

parts.note: Buick is an American car make

explanation.surface: Someone lost a dollar coin down the seat of a US car.
explanation.definitionFit: Buck is common American slang for a dollar, the US unit of currency.

clue.text: Foolish shot by Surrey's tail-ender

parts.note: to have a shot at something is to have a go
a work by someone is a work of theirs, as in a play of Shakespeare's

indicators.note: in cricket the tail-enders bat last, so this picks the final letter

parts.note: the county name taken for its last letter

explanation.surface: A daft stroke played by Surrey's last batsman in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is an English county with a famous cricket side; a tail-ender is one of the weak batsmen who go in last.
explanation.definitionFit: Goofy is informal for silly or daft, describing behaviour that is clownish and ridiculous.

clue.text: Noise from animal at home that's piercing all right

indicators.note: the at-home word pierces the all-right word, going inside it

parts.note: OK means all right
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A shrill animal noise heard at home that is acceptably piercing.
explanation.definitionFit: Oink is the grunting sound a pig makes, imitative of the animal's call.

clue.text: Senior covered with juice at school, tricked with a lemon?

indicators.note: the word for senior is wrapped inside the word for juice

parts.note: sap is the juice of a plant
old means senior in years
to be up is to be at university or school, in residence

explanation.surface: An older pupil gets drenched in juice at school, fooled with a lemon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lemon' tempts you towards juice, but here it means a dud purchase.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sold a pup is to be swindled into buying something worthless; a lemon is slang for a defective item.

clue.text: Work in tech with exotic people

indicators.note: the letters are worked, kneaded into a different order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An IT job alongside people from foreign lands.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnic describes things relating to a minority cultural group, or foreign food and fashion seen as exotic.

clue.text: Professionally qualified cleaner wants stool picked up

parts.note: a char or charwoman is a cleaning lady

indicators.note: heard, as on a radio, so this indicates a sound-alike

parts.note: stool in the medical sense is faeces

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady needs a stool lifted while she works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stool' looks like a seat to be picked up; here it is the bodily kind, and the second half of the answer sounds like it.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartered describes accountants, surveyors and engineers who hold a professional body's royal charter qualification.

clue.text: Excited spaniel who listened to papa

indicators.note: heard rather than read, so the words are replaced by a sound-alike

parts.note: a cocker is a cocker spaniel, and the pair 'cocker who' said aloud in a British accent gives the sound

explanation.surface: An eager spaniel that obeyed its father.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech, cocker who sounds like the first part of the answer; P is papa in the NATO alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Cock-a-hoop means jubilant or elated, in high spirits after some success.

clue.text: Grooming kit to work on frisky setter, having tail clipped

indicators.note: in this down clue one piece is placed on top of the other

parts.note: to toil is to work hard

indicators.note: lively and skittish, so the letters jump into a new order
the last letter is cut off, like docking a dog's tail

parts.note: taken as written for its letters

explanation.surface: Pet-grooming tools for working on a lively setter dog, including a tail trim.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog in the surface is a setter, but the grooming kit is for people.
explanation.definitionFit: A toilet set is a matching collection of brush, comb and mirror for personal grooming at the dressing table.

clue.text: Black dog let out indiscreetly

parts.note: a lab is a Labrador retriever

explanation.surface: A black dog was let off the lead without care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let out' suggests a dog released, but the definition means revealing a secret.
explanation.definitionFit: To blab is to reveal secrets thoughtlessly, gossiping about what should be kept private.

clue.text: Live event broadcast including house music

parts.note: to be is to exist or live

indicators.note: the rearranged letters take the house abbreviation inside them
scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be scattered

explanation.surface: A live concert broadcast which features house, the dance genre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House music' looks like a single genre, but house is a separate piece and music the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer stands for his works by metonymy, as when someone says they're listening to some of his symphonies.

clue.text: Sore from always carrying children

indicators.note: the word for always carries the children inside it

parts.note: ay, also spelt aye, is an old and Scottish word for ever or always

explanation.surface: Aching all over from constantly holding the kids.
explanation.definitionFit: Achy means suffering a dull persistent pain, the same as sore or aching.

clue.text: Untruthful, popular, Conservative, cycling minister

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: letters move round from one end of the word to the other, like a wheel turning

parts.note: a rector is a parish minister

explanation.surface: A lying, well-liked Tory clergyman out on his bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests a vicar on a bicycle, but it moves the last two letters to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Incorrect means wrong or not true, so an untruthful statement is an inaccurate one.

clue.text: Young Scot's story with hidden booty?

indicators.note: the booty is concealed inside the story

parts.note: a story can be a lie, a fib
booty is slang for buttocks, and ass is the American word

explanation.surface: A girl from Scotland tells a tale with buried treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booty' suggests pirate treasure; here it is the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassie is the Scottish word for a girl, a young female, diminutive of lass.

clue.text: White covered by this now yellow

indicators.note: the answer is concealed by the letters of the following words

parts.note: the run of letters sits across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Something white that has been turned yellow now, perhaps by a stain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the yellow snow joke without saying it.
explanation.definitionFit: Snowy means pure white like freshly fallen snow.

clue.text: Forbidden drink, son finishes playing darts

parts.note: something out is not allowed
a shot is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A banned drink with a son ending a game of darts.
explanation.definitionFit: In darts an outshot is the throw that finishes a leg, checking out on a double.

clue.text: Question Charlie with sunhat on

indicators.note: in this down clue the sunhat is placed on top of the letter for Charlie

parts.note: a topi is a pith helmet worn against the sun

explanation.surface: Asking Charlie with his sunhat on.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is a subject or issue under discussion, the matter or question in hand.

clue.text: Tread right in stuff

indicators.note: the letter for right goes inside the word for stuff

parts.note: to tamp is to pack something down firmly

explanation.surface: Stepping right in something unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily, tread with firm footsteps.

clue.text: Sprite and doughnut for 24

definitions.note: refers to the answer at 24 down, in its sense of a vagrant

parts.note: a hob is a hobgoblin or sprite
the ring shape of a doughnut looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Sharing a fizzy drink and a doughnut with a homeless person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprite' looks like the lemonade brand next to a snack, but it is a goblin.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobo is an American term for a wandering vagrant, the same as the other answer's noun sense.

clue.text: Scud shed tears after introduction to Sid

indicators.note: the crying word comes after the opening letter
the introduction is the very first letter of the name

parts.note: the name supplies only its opening letter
to weep is to cry

explanation.surface: A man called Sid cried after his introduction to a scud missile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scud' suggests the missile, but it is a verb meaning to move fast.
explanation.definitionFit: To scud is to move swiftly and smoothly, as clouds do, and to sweep is likewise to glide quickly.

clue.text: Some massive Alsatians butchered young cattle

definitions.note: meat from calves, so the definition reads as a noun phrase

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used, a run concealed inside the words

parts.note: the answer straddles the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Large guard dogs savaged some calves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butchered' looks like the anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Veal is the meat of calves, slaughtered young cattle prepared for the table.

clue.text: English toy poodle's coat tangled in cactus

indicators.note: a coat is the outside layer, so only the outer letters of the dog's name are kept

parts.note: the dog poodle, its 's a possessive

indicators.note: tangled means knotted out of order, so the letters of toy are rearranged

explanation.surface: A British toy poodle's fur gets snagged in a prickly plant.
explanation.walkthrough: PE, the outside of POODLE, comes first; 'tangled' gives YOT from TOY, and E for English ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: Peyote is a small spineless Mexican cactus whose buttons are hallucinogenic.

clue.text: Article in crib possibly a bed cover

indicators.note: the article goes inside the word for crib

parts.note: to crib is to copy someone else's work
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An item in a baby's cot, perhaps a blanket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crib' suggests a cot, matching the bed cover; it means copy, as in cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: A canopy is a cloth covering hung above a four-poster bed.
